/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Police funding rises to historic £18.5bn, Home Office says
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.bodyHtml:
Police funding has risen by £2bn since the last election, taking it to a historic high of £18.5bn this year, the Home Office says, as it works on a new approach to how that money is shared out.

A spokesperson for the Home Office said: “Since the election, we have increased funding to policing by £2bn. Police force funding this year is at a historic high of £18.5bn.

“We have established the financial resilience framework to ensure a consistent approach to assessing financial resilience in policing.

“We are also reviewing the police funding formula to ensure the system is fair and continues to prioritise public safety. The new approach to funding will be brought in as part of our reforms to police structures.”

But police chiefs say officers are “retreating from the streets” amid the worst financial crisis in decades, which has left nine forces seeking exceptional financial support (EFS) from the government.

Paul Sanford, the chief constable of Norfolk police and the finance lead for the National Police Chiefs’ Council (NPCC), said exceptional financial support was needed if forces across England and Wales were to remain operationally viable.

He named the nine forces as Durham, Cleveland, Greater Manchester, Wiltshire, Bedfordshire, South Yorkshire, Gloucestershire, Lincolnshire and Norfolk.

The Home Office, which will decide whether or not the forces will get extra money – or whether the relevant councils will be allowed to charge taxpayers more – declined to confirm how many forces had applied for support.

The government argues it has already given forces extra money in real terms, but police chiefs say demands on them have risen, as have population numbers.

When Labour came to power in July 2024, officer numbers stood at 148,536, according to June 2024 figures. By March this year, the figure had fallen to 147,822, and senior officers expect it to fall further.

Sanford told the Guardian: “Demand has gone up, population has increased. There is a growth in complex cases, sexual offending and historic inquiries, and civil orders. All of those are the right thing to do, but they’ve not come with the funding required.

“That is why you see the retreat from the streets. Policing is in worse financial shape now than it has been for decades.

“Those forces who have applied for EFS believe that they are close to the tipping point where the ability to deliver core services can no longer be sustained.”

One of the factors affecting forces’ budgets is the government’s early release scheme for prisoners, intended to ease the overcrowding crisis in jails. The NPCC has predicted this will lead to a rise in crime of up to 6%, with a consequent need for officers to respond.

Police chiefs now say the projected funding gap for forces by 2030 has rocketed from £3bn to £4.3bn.

They point to the use of reserves worth £300m by 43 forces in the last year as a sign of increasing financial distress, saying that while some of this was used for investment, some was needed to maintain services.

Trevor Rodenhurst, the chief constable of Bedfordshire, said of the application for additional government support: “If I don’t get the money, the impact would be to degrade services.”

The Bedfordshire force has 1,486 officers, which Rodenhurst believes is hundreds fewer than it needs. He says it is getting a thousand more 999 calls a month this year compared with last year.

Catherine Roper, the chief constable of Wiltshire, said: “We’ve taken the efficiencies we can out of the system. The wiggle room we have is leaner.”

Privately, chiefs believe that Labour’s election promise of 13,000 new officers by 2029 has no chance of being met.

The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, will face the NPCC this week at its annual conference. Some of its members agree with the government that radical police reform, such as cutting the number of forces from 43 to nine, will free up hundreds of millions of pounds for fighting crime. But any projected savings remain years away.

Stephen Watson, the chief constable of Greater Manchester, who is highly regarded by the prime minister, said: “The one thing that everyone agrees is that the policing system has been underinvested in for years and that the public are rightly demanding improvements now.

“But there is no point in the service being seen to whine about what we haven’t got when it is a racing certainty, given the state of our public finances, that no great slug of additional general funding is going to drop into policing anytime soon. Nor is the Treasury likely to be keen on directing even targeted investment into an unreformed service.”

The Conservative-led government that came to power in 2010 cut police funding as part of its austerity programme, with 20,000 officers lost before ministers reversed course.

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: Milburn blueprint could halve youth unemployment within a decade
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.bodyHtml:
Publishing a blueprint for change in a highly anticipated review, the report calls on the government to launch a sweeping shake-up of welfare, education, health and employment policy with the aim to ensure every young person has the chance to earn or learn.

If adopted by the government, Britain could halve the number of young people neither earning nor learning, helping about 600,000 more under-25s into education, employment or training each year by 2036, according to the review.

Andy Burnham is being urged to spend billions of pounds on a “new deal” for the next generation that would fund guaranteed jobs support for young people to offset a radical cut in benefits.

In a watershed report on Britain’s youth jobs crisis, Alan Milburn, the Tony Blair-era health secretary, said the country was at a “fork in the road” after a surge in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost a million.

He said ministers had a choice to either carry on down a path of state and market failure or adopt a 10-year plan with an ambition to eradicate long-term youth unemployment.

Milburn’s report comes as Britain’s young bear the brunt of rising joblessness as employers freeze their hiring plans amid the fallout from the war in the Middle East. Coupled with the legacies of the Covid pandemic and austerity, and a rise in mental ill-health and as AI upends the jobs market, the UK’s Neet rate has reached 13% – the highest level since 2014. Milburn said that rate could be lowered to 5% by 2036.

However, central to his plan would be a controversial shake-up of Britain’s benefits system to approach the under-25s as wholly separate from the working-age population at large.

Urging the prime minister not to shy away from welfare reform – after Keir Starmer was forced into a humiliating climbdown over a plan to cut disability benefits amid pressure from Labour MPs – Milburn warned the future of the next generation depended on the government making changes.

At a press conference in London on Tuesday to mark the launch of his report, he is expected to say: “It is time for a new settlement that makes work not welfare the future for the next generation.”

But Milburn also warned that crude benefit cuts would not work, arguing that changes would need upfront investment.

Burnham pledged on Sunday to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment. Writing in the Guardian, he promised that changes to benefits he was considering in response to Milburn’s review would only be accompanied by a “root and branch rethink” of youth support.

At the heart of Milburn’s blueprint would be the creation of an entirely new welfare system for young people, involving tougher eligibility criteria than for older claimants. In exchange, however, there would be a drastic step-change in support to help young people find work.

This would involve some young people with health conditions and disabilities losing access to current benefits, although they would be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment. Those with the most profound health conditions who would be unable ever to work would still get more generous financial support.

To counterbalance the changes, Milburn said upfront investment to create a new “youth opportunity service” in England should be created to deliver a drastic boost in support for young people.

Accountable to regional mayors and local leaders, the service would combine employment, careers, health and practical support. Young people would receive a personalised participation plan and a named adviser, with access to support guaranteed by two new legal guarantees.

While education, skills and health policies are devolved in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland, Milburn will say at the report launch that the underlying principles in his report should also apply.

Analysis in Milburn’s report shows that for every £1 spent on helping young people into work or education, the state spent £25 on youth benefits last year. Under his proposals that figure would be rebalanced to £2 to £1, bringing Britain closer into line with the ratios in other European countries.

The changes will, however, raise fears among some Labour MPs as well as charities and campaigners that slashing youth benefits could result in plunging more young people into poverty, particularly for those who require additional financial support to manage health conditions.

As Milburn prepared to launch his review, backbenchers from the left of the party – including Nadia Whittome, Bell Ribeiro-Addy, John McDonnell, Apsana Begum, Clive Lewis and Richard Burgon – warned in a letter that an entire generation risked becoming disconnected from work and wider society.

“What young people need is not more punishment, but more opportunity,” the signatories wrote, warning that an approach relying on benefit cuts “risks further disenfranchising young people who are already struggling”.

They added: “Placing young people under threat of losing essential financial support does not address the shortage of good-quality jobs, the barriers facing disabled young people, or the lack of meaningful routes into employment.”

In a bid to ease concerns among Labour MPs after last year’s welfare rebellion threatened to rupture the party and arguably began Starmer’s downfall, Milburn held meetings with MPs on Monday alongside the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden.

McFadden told backbenchers: “What is proposed is a new settlement for young people. This is not last year’s proposal with better PR. It’s about bringing together the help young people need in one place – treating them as a person not a departmental client.”

Milburn said Britain had faced a Neet problem for 25 years and had never made a plan to end it before. “We are at a fork in the road and half measures will not do. A complete system reset is needed. A lost generation is not inevitable. A work generation is possible.”

Labour has faced fierce criticism from business groups who say its decisions – including tax increases and a rising minimum wage – have added to Britain’s crisis in youth jobs, while the Conservatives and Reform have pushed for a tougher approach on benefits.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said Milburn’s review was “too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state”.

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years,” she said. “Even so, there’s a long road ahead to see if it can get past welfare-loving Labour MPs.”

/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.bodyHtml:
The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he was not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Brand's wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

Brand could face sanctions, ranging from an extension of his sentence to the loss of privileges such as access to a telephone for a limited period, if he is found to have broken the rules.

It is understood a prisoner will be deemed to have broken the rules if they provide comments to a family member that they know will be published.

Asked about the comments, the prime minister's official spokesperson said: "This is clearly appalling and is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules.

"Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances. Prisoners cannot get around these rules by having someone else publish their comments … This is being urgently investigated. We expect action to be taken if the rules have been broken."

Brand, 51, is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term after he was convicted of one count of rape and three sexual assaults at Southwark crown court on 5 November.

In his message, Brand said he had been moved from the category-B Wandsworth prison in south-west London to the category-C HMP Littlehey in Cambridgeshire, a prison for men convicted of sexual offences.

Reading the message from a notebook, Laura Brand said: "As you know, I am not guilty for the offences I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening.

"I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey, little as in small, and hey as in hey, I'm in the biggest sex offenders' prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone.

"I don't know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me, let us all love, pray for and forgive one another as God forgave us."

Prisoners are allowed to protest their innocence, so no criminal offence has been committed by releasing the podcast, though they are not allowed to make statements from jail that cause distress to victims, and heavy restrictions apply to speaking to the media.

According to official guidance on prisoner access to the media, a prison governor must decide whether to permit it, and must consider that "serious distress to victims of the prisoner and/or outrage to public sensibilities is not likely to result from the broadcast. This is likely to occur if, for example, the prisoner's crimes or conduct are recent, notorious or horrific."

The rules state that correspondence likely to be published or broadcast "must not contain material about the prisoner's own crime or past offences or those of others, except where it consists of serious representations about conviction or sentence".

Mia Latter, who alleges she was raped by Brand when she was 16 and has waived her right to anonymity, said his message was an "insult" to his victims and questioned why YouTube had allowed the video to be shared.

She told The Jeremy Vine Show on Channel 5: "I was shocked that YouTube put it out, because I feel like they have some kind of responsibility not to let these things be broadcast.

"And, it was an insult to all the women that stood trial, and it was an insult to the jurors that gave their time. It's an insult to the criminal justice system."

In July 2022, prisoner Charles Bronson said he was given a 28-day phone ban after sending an unauthorised voice note from his cell at HMP Woodhill.

Prison sources said it was not yet clear whether Brand had broken a rule because the message was posted by Brand's wife, not by him, and the material may have been written before conviction. "There are a lot of possible scenarios, and the full facts are still to emerge," a source said.

Responding to the video on Monday, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, told Sky News: "His crimes are heinous and awful. I think it's revolting, by the way, that he shows no remorse today in his comments. No remorse, no sympathy for the victims. Just disgusting comments."

According to official guidance, prisoners are expected to make a formal application through their governor if they wish to contact the media.

Allegations against Brand and fellow comedian David Walliams have prompted conversations about introducing a staggered age of consent.

The Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said there was "some common sense" in the idea, but expressed doubts about how it could be enforced.

"I do think that there's some common sense there in terms of a staggered age of consent. My issue is with how we will enforce it," she told a press conference. Walliams denies wrongdoing.

/film/2026/nov/16/new-james-bond-announc.headline: Robert Pattinson lands the role of a lifetime as new 007
/film/2026/nov/16/new-james-bond-announc.bodyHtml:
Robert Pattinson has been announced as the successor to Daniel Craig, becoming the seventh actor to play the role in an official Bond movie.

The news was revealed on the official James Bond social media accounts on Monday. All earlier content was abruptly wiped from 007 on X and Instagram just before 3pm GMT and a repeating message typed out: "Identity confirmed."

The film studio then released a first photo of the actor in Bond's trademark tuxedo with a press release confirming the news and saying Pattinson's casting will "usher in a new era for one of cinema's most celebrated characters".

In a statement Pattinson said: "James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime … To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement."

The announcement came after a drawn-out casting process, in which Pattinson was understood to be on a five-strong shortlist, which included Josh O'Connor and Callum Turner. On Friday suggestions emerged that Pattinson had been offered more favourable contract terms than his rivals, fuelling rumours that he was the strong favourite for the role.

Craig's final film as Bond was No Time to Die, released in 2021 after being delayed due to the Covid pandemic. The narrative for the 25th film in the series lent the franchise a sense of closure, with Bond apparently dying before a title card promised: "James Bond will return".

Craig made five Bond films in total, starting with Casino Royale in 2006. During his tenure the franchise became a box-office record-breaker, with 2012's Skyfall alone taking $1.1bn globally.

Pattinson, 40, is due to appear in the next Bond film, the 26th in the franchise (although two "unofficial" entries, Casino Royale in 1967 and Never Say Never Again in 1983, take the total to 28). The as yet untitled project will be the first to be shot since Amazon-MGM Studios purchased the rights to the series for more than $1bn in 2025 from Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson, heirs to original producer Albert "Cubby" Broccoli and longtime stewards of the Bond films.

Harry Potter producer David Heyman and Spider-Man producer Amy Pascal will oversee the franchise, while the Dune trilogy's Denis Villeneuve will direct and Peaky Blinders' Steven Knight is writing the script.

Pattinson has demonstrated his versatility across a wide variety of roles, earning a reputation as an actor with broad enough appeal to support major blockbuster films while retaining artistic credibility with offbeat and unlikely choices. He first came to notice in 2005 as Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire, and achieved superstardom opposite Kristen Stewart as vampire Edward Cullen in the Twilight film series. He appeared in films directed by David Cronenberg (Cosmopolis, Maps to the Stars), Robert Eggers (The Lighthouse) and Lynne Ramsay (Die My Love), and returned to franchise film-making with The Batman in 2022.

The first actor to play Bond on the big screen was Edinburgh-born Sean Connery in 1962's Dr No. So successful was the film that Connery returned to make four further films over the next five years, which are considered by many to be some of the franchise's finest: From Russia With Love, Goldfinger, Thunderball and You Only Live Twice. Bond creator Ian Fleming's preference for the role, the English actor David Niven, starred in the non-canonical Casino Royale (1967), while the Australian model George Lazenby joined for one outing, 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service, before Connery rejoined for Diamonds Are Forever (1971).

Roger Moore then lent the series a more ironic spin for his seven films between 1973 and 1985, which include The Spy Who Loved Me, Moonraker and Octopussy. The role then went to British actor Timothy Dalton for two films in the late 1980s; a six-year gap preceded Irish actor Pierce Brosnan's debut in 1995 in GoldenEye. He shot four films as 007 before Craig's tenure began.

The official James Bond films have so far made a total of $7.8bn, making the franchise the fifth highest-grossing in history. Proceeds from merchandise and sponsorship deals are estimated to far exceed that figure.

Catherine Shoard will be in the comments from 5.30pm today to answer readers' questions about the casting.

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: Home Office points to Denmark in bid to speed up asylum removals
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.bodyHtml:
The overhaul follows a similar approach to the system that Denmark operates successfully, the Home Office says.

The number of migrants awaiting removal in Denmark was cut from more than 2,185 cases at the end of 2020 to fewer than 1,000 at the end of 2025.

Under the changes, asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal, a move refugee charities have condemned as “distressing”.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow immigration enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.

Mahmood has tabled an amendment to the immigration and asylum bill that will scrap the five-day timeframe.

Officials would instead be given a six-month period to remove refused asylum seekers and rejected migrants before further notice is required, the Home Office said.

Currently, enforced returns for rejected claimants can only take place after a minimum notice period of five working days, which can allow people to launch other legal interventions or prepare themselves for removal.

There are currently exceptions to the five-day notice period for removals, such as where the removal was disrupted by the individual or was cancelled due to bad weather. In these scenarios, removal can be attempted again without further notice for 21 days.

This timeframe will now be increased to six months under reforms in the bill, which returns to the House of Commons for report stage and third reading on 17 November.

The bill will also introduce a new immigration appeals authority with the aim of speeding up removals and changes to how human rights and modern slavery laws are applied to asylum applications to root out what the government described as “vexatious” claims.

Ministers hope the bill will bring into force proposals that will create a firm but fair asylum system, and which will reduce the pull factors driving illegal immigration.

Under other reforms, the responsibility to make modern slavery decisions for children will be devolved to local safeguarding partners.

This will ensure professionals who already support the child, and are closest to the child, are making the decisions for their future, the Home Office said.

The UK has increased the number of removals since Labour came to power, but faces huge backlogs in asylum applications. As of 30 June 2026, 40,168 people were waiting for an initial asylum decision in the UK. The number of refused applications hit more than 90,000 in the same month, breaking previous records.

Anna Turley, the minister for border security and asylum, said: “This government is ramping up removals of those with no right to be here, with over 80,000 illegal migrants and foreign nationals returned since the general election.

“Now we are ensuring those migrants who have exhausted their right to appeal can be removed promptly, rather than being given an opportunity to frustrate their legitimate removal from this country.”

Imran Hussain, the director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, condemned the change.

“We must treat people with dignity. Removing people at such short notice will cause unnecessary distress and anxiety,” he said.

“We also need to look at the evidence of what works. The reality is that voluntary removals are far more effective at removing people than enforced returns. If you assist people to return with dignity, many will take that option, at far lower cost to the taxpayer.”

Louise Calvey, the executive director at Asylum Matters, said: “People deserve a fair chance to make their claim for help and sanctuary, but forcibly removing people from the country so they don’t get a chance to make their claims won’t fix that.

“Right now, 63% of the population don’t have access to an asylum legal aid provider. What that means is people are attempting to navigate a horrendously complex and hostile system in a new country, often in a second language. In that environment, many people may not have had the proper advice in initial claims, so many who make further claims are found to have a genuine need for support.

“Expelling people from the country to ensure we never get to hear their legitimate claims is nothing to be proud of – it will lead to real injustices.”

/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/16/woman-accusing.headline: Second woman backs call for a staggered age of consent
/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/16/woman-accusing.bodyHtml:
A woman who has accused David Walliams of grooming her has said she supports a staggered age of consent.

Alex said she would have saved herself “a lot of trauma” if a staggered age of consent had been in place when she was a teenager.

Alex was speaking out after a woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent. Mia Latter told the Sunday Times she was in an abusive three-month relationship with Brand when he was 30 and she was 16.

She has called on the UK government to introduce a law that would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Walliams, 55, has been accused of using his power and celebrity status to prey on young women and teenagers for sex, a joint investigation by the Guardian and ITV News has found.

Alex has alleged she was 15 and studying for her GCSEs when she first met Walliams, one of Britain’s best-known television personalities and top-selling children’s authors. She has alleged they began having sex when she was 17 and Walliams was 34.

“As a parent myself now, I would absolutely love for there to be a change of law. It’s something that is incredibly close to my heart, and I would feel very, very proud and happy if this could get over the line,” she told the Guardian and ITV News.

“It would protect everyone … from people that can abuse the law as it currently stands. I think it’s really important that teenagers are able to have relationships with each other. I think that the staggered element to it, I think works really well.”

Last week, Alex told the Guardian and ITV News that she was “groomed” by Walliams. “I never said no … but I felt unable to say anything or have any control in that situation once I was with him,” she said.

“OK, it’s legal to have sex when you’re 17, 18, 16 even, but the context of who you’re having sex with – if that person is double your age, if that person has known you from a young age and promised you things and is in a much bigger position of power than you, both in age, in work, in finance, in stature and size, like, everything, I really don’t think that’s OK.”

On Monday, Alex backed calls for a change in the law to “make it a lot harder for predators to act”.

She said she would have had a different perspective on Walliams’ behaviour had the law already been in place when she was a teenager.

“I grew up in a culture where it was normalised,” she said. “There were people saying to me at the time that this feels really wrong, but it was a bit more accepted, and it still happened more. And I think if I grew up in a world where [I] knew that that was illegal, and it was more clear that that shouldn’t have been happening, and that was wrong, then I think that I would have been a lot more wary of that and scared by it, and probably seen it more clearly for what it was at a younger age.

“I feel like if we can make the children of today know and understand from a young age that’s illegal, that’s against the law, that that person shouldn’t be talking to you in that way, shouldn’t be engaging with you in that way, and certainly shouldn’t be acting on it, it would make you pause and hope and I think it would definitely stop a lot of incidents happening.”

Walliams’ lawyers have said the suggestion he groomed Alex is false and that she did not raise, and he did not believe, that she had any concerns about the sex at the time. The lawyers add that Walliams was mortified to learn that their brief, consensual relationship had caused her sadness. Walliams has denied all the allegations against him.

The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. Samaritans can be contacted on freephone 116 123. Other international helplines are available for people affected by sexual abuse, childhood abuse, and people in crisis.

/politics/2026/nov/16/people-behind-vote.headline: Badenoch and Miliband resist calls to reopen the Brexit argument
/politics/2026/nov/16/people-behind-vote.bodyHtml:
At a press conference on Monday, the Conservative leader, Kemi Badenoch, said she would not engage with campaigning on Brexit. “We need to stop obsessing about Europe and whether to be in or out, and actually get on with doing the things that we are elected to do,” she said.

“Sort out the economy, fund our defence, cut welfare, get jobs for people, make sure that businesses can create those jobs. We don’t need to be in the EU to do any of that.”

Badenoch said she believed that voters would decide to stay out of the EU, but added: “I’m not interested in engaging in this debate. They [Labour] want to distract us by making us talk about Brexit, because if we’re talking about that then we’re not talking about the government’s failures. I’m not falling for that trick.”

Speaking on Monday before a crunch EU summit where Burnham hopes to clinch a new deal with the EU on food and drink and emissions trading, as well as a youth mobility deal, the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said the government respected the 2016 result.

“What we’re very focused on is actually what’s in front of us, which is this summit and how we can just help the British people in the situation we face,” he told BBC Breakfast.

The Brexit wars were a bitter period in political history, fraught with tension and badmouthing – and that was just between the different leave campaigns.

Now as a new incarnation of Dominic Cummings’ Vote Leave looks set to re-enter the political fray, so too does a rival anti-EU campaign from the team behind Leave.EU, who ran their own unofficial campaign backed by Nigel Farage.

This time, both have vowed to be cordial with each other, but in 2016 there were significant creative differences.

Many of the names are the same. Oliver Lewis, a veteran of Vote Leave who was a Brexit negotiator under Boris Johnson, will chair Stay Out, a new campaign group backed by the former cabinet minister Michael Gove and under the interested eye of Cummings, though he has no formal role.

The launch of the campaign video – which claimed the costs of rejoining the EU would be £750m a week, and featured footage of recent riots in France and Spain and warnings about unchecked migration – caught No 10 off-guard.

On Monday they were joined by the launch of a parallel campaign from Andy Wigmore’s Leave.EU, which will be called Enough Official. Wigmore told the Telegraph he wanted to work with Lewis’s group. “There’s no split camps this time,” he said. “We’re all going to support each other, and we will support anyone who’s going to fight this.”

A number of high-profile political figures seem to be willing to re-enter the fray from retirement, including Johnson. The former prime minister and leave campaigner told the Telegraph it would be “madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority … [Andy Burnham] won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

Johnson hinted to the paper that he would be willing to be part of a campaign to stay out of the bloc. “There are plenty of people who are only too happy to make the points I’ve made – but I will of course make the points that I’ve made,” he said.

One senior campaigner said it was an irresistible opportunity for many former political advisers who were now out of Westminster politics. “They’re very effective guys that have been sitting around waiting for a chance to make themselves useful. A lot of talent on the right is currently off making money or kicking their feet. Rejoining is the one thing that will bring them back,” they said.

Veterans of both Vote Leave and Leave.EU are split between those who are willing to campaign to stay out and others who believe the political landscape is now far more uncertain.

One senior figure said they “had PTSD” from the Brexit period and vowed to steer clear. “I think that is exactly the reason why the prime minister should not be reopening this debate, but I don’t think anyone should be under any illusion it would be an easy win for either side.”

Another campaign veteran said both pro- and anti-EU campaigns would find it more difficult to get businesses to pick a side or to get public figures involved. “I think that many are scarred from previous involvement, but this would work in both directions,” they said.

Several of those involved in the campaigns said they expected serving politicians to be kept at arm’s length – including Farage.

Launching the campaign over the weekend, Lewis said Stay Out would make the argument on the economics and on immigration – and on the risk of reopening divisions.

“The bloc is also getting bigger, with Albania, Moldova and the western Balkans all in the queue to join, and Brussels wants Britain back in as one of the few countries rich enough to pay for it,” he said. “The country has had enough of arguing about Europe, and it is time to move on and spend our money on our own priorities.”

Gove, who was a co-convener of Vote Leave, said a move towards rejoining would “commit the country to another decade of fractious negotiations and a return to the divisions we have spent years putting behind us, at the very moment people are desperate for Westminster to get on with delivering on their priorities.”

/media/2026/nov/16/emma-barnett-steps-do.headline: Emma Barnett moves from Today to front bold new BBC show
/media/2026/nov/16/emma-barnett-steps-do.bodyHtml:
Barnett will stay with the BBC, fronting a new show that will also be available on YouTube, as well as BBC iPlayer and the corporation’s BBC Sounds app. Exact details have not been announced, but it is expected to be a longform interview format.

The BBC has confirmed Emma Barnett is stepping down as a presenter of Radio 4’s Today programme, setting off the broadcaster’s latest search for a new name to co-host its flagship news programme.

The official announcement came after months of speculation about Barnett’s future on the show. Her last appearance will be broadcast on Wednesday.

Her departure comes just months after fellow presenter Amol Rajan left the show, opting instead to launch his own project, Amol Rajan Connection, on YouTube.

Barnett said it had been “incredible to talk to the mighty Radio 4 listeners” over the last six years.

“Having proudly hosted Woman’s Hour and now the Today programme I’ve had the rare pleasure of hosting nearly every hour of the morning on this truly unique and special radio network,” she said. “But it’s not goodbye to the BBC audience I value so greatly because I have something else for them that I hope will add something meaningful and entertaining to their lives.

“Over the last nine months, we have been creating a bold new BBC show which will launch at the start of 2027. Watch this space and look ready. I am.”

Barnett joined Today in 2024. Her short tenure had been the subject of rumours about clashes with fellow presenters – denied by her co-host Nick Robinson. Some insiders also believe she suffered from indecision at the BBC about the direction of the show.

Barnett’s previous success at BBC Radio 5 Live came from creating a show driven by her personal style, but she has also faced criticism for bringing personality to the Today programme.

A renewed search will begin for a new face to present alongside the rotating line-up of Robinson, Justin Webb and Anna Foster. Attempts to replace Rajan were ended after bosses decided to reduce Today’s presenting roster as part of BBC cuts.

Katie Razzall, the BBC’s culture and media editor, is thought to be well placed to take on the job. BBC executives have been impressed with how the Media Show, which Razzall presents on Radio 4, generates stories and works on digital platforms.

Katya Adler, the BBC’s Europe editor who has stepped in as a guest presenter of Today, is also seen as a possible replacement.

ITV’s Julie Etchingham and Sky News’s Sophy Ridge have recently been cited as potential outside candidates for the show.

Etchingham moderated the first election debate between Rishi Sunak and Keir Starmer and was regarded by many viewers as the real winner from the encounter. Ridge was named presenter of the year at the Royal Television Society awards last year and has previously worked with John McAndrew, the director of programmes for BBC News.

Despite the fact that audiences have fragmented as a result of the rise of digital platforms and the draw of social media, the Today programme has retained its status as one of the BBC’s prize assets. It has more than 5 million listeners a week.

Rebecca Keating, the editor of Today, said of Barnett: “Emma has brought enormous energy to Today and a keen focus on our listeners.

“She has a track record of telling stories of personal hardship that influence public debate but is also equally at home interviewing British icons like Dame Judi Dench. We will miss her generous tea making and wish her every success in her new venture.”
